da-2026-2-da-43.approach: Use the definition: a real square matrix is orthogonal when its columns (equivalently rows) form an orthonormal set, which is exactly $Q^TQ = I$; for a square matrix this forces $QQ^T = I$ too. Test each option against that definition or a quick counterexample.

steps.title: Write the definition in matrix form
steps.body:
Let $q_1,\dots,q_n$ be the columns of $Q$. The $(i,j)$ entry of $Q^TQ$ is $q_i^Tq_j$. Orthonormal columns mean $q_i^Tq_j = 1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, i.e.
$$Q^TQ = I.$$

steps.title: A one-sided inverse of a square matrix is two-sided
steps.body: $Q^TQ = I$ says $Q^T$ is a left inverse of the square matrix $Q$, so $Q$ is invertible with $Q^{-1} = Q^T$. Then $QQ^T = QQ^{-1} = I$ as well. Hence orthogonal $\iff Q^TQ = QQ^T = I$ — option (C).

steps.title: Reject the other conditions with counterexamples
steps.body:
- (A) $Q=Q^T$ is **symmetry**: $\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ is symmetric but $Q^TQ = 4I \ne I$.
- (B) $Q^2=Q$ is **idempotence** (a projection): $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ satisfies it but is singular, so not orthogonal.
- (D) $\det(Q)=0$ is impossible: $\det(Q^TQ)=\det(Q)^2=\det I = 1$, so $\det Q = \pm 1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: That is the definition of a symmetric matrix; $2I$ is symmetric but $(2I)^T(2I) = 4I \ne I$.
That defines an idempotent (projection) matrix; $\mathrm{diag}(1,0)$ is idempotent yet singular.

Orthogonal matrices have $\det Q = \pm 1$ (from $\det(Q)^2 = 1$), never $0$.

steps.body: For $X\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$. Here $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$.

steps.body:

$$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 3^2 \times 4 = 9 \times 4 = 36.$$

steps.body: The mean shifts and scales: $E[Y] = 3E[X] + 5 = 3 \times 4 + 5 = 17$. The variance ignores the shift $+5$ and squares the scale: $36$. So $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 36$ — option (A).

steps.title: Write the given schema
steps.body: Premises: $P$ and $P\to Q$. Conclusion: $Q$. In symbols $\dfrac{P,\;\; P\to Q}{Q}$.

steps.title: Check it is valid and name it
steps.body: The only row of the truth table with $P = T$ and $(P\to Q) = T$ has $Q = T$ (if $Q$ were $F$, $P\to Q$ would be $F$). So the inference is valid; this rule is **Modus Ponens** — option (A).

steps.body:
| Rule | Premises | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Modus Ponens | $P,\; P\to Q$ | $Q$ |
| Modus Tollens | $\neg Q,\; P\to Q$ | $\neg P$ |
| Hypothetical Syllogism | $P\to Q,\; Q\to R$ | $P\to R$ |
| Resolution | $P\lor Q,\; \neg P\lor R$ | $Q\lor R$ |

Modus tollens goes the other way: from $\neg Q$ and $P\to Q$ it derives $\neg P$.

da-2026-2-da-46.approach: A moving average needs a *window* that slides over ordered rows while every row is kept — that is a window (analytic) function, written with an `OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …)` clause. Aggregating clauses (GROUP BY, HAVING, PIVOT) collapse rows instead.

steps.title: What a moving average requires
steps.body: For every row (say, every day of every store) we want the average of a few neighbouring rows in time order. The output must have **one row per input row**, so grouping operators that collapse rows cannot do it.

steps.title: The window clause
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT store, day, sales,
       AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY store ORDER BY day
                        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7
FROM daily_sales;
```
`PARTITION BY` splits the rows into independent windows (per store), `ORDER BY` fixes the order in which the frame slides, and the frame clause sets the window width. This is option (A).

steps.title: Why the others do not fit
steps.body: `GROUP BY ROLLUP` produces subtotal/grand-total rows (hierarchical aggregation); `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation; `PIVOT … FOR …` rotates row values into columns. None defines a rolling window.

optionAnalysis.reason: Window-function clause: partitions rows and orders them so a frame can slide — exactly a rolling window for moving averages.
`ROLLUP` adds super-aggregate (subtotal) rows along a hierarchy; it collapses rows and has no notion of a sliding window.
`HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` only filters groups produced by `GROUP BY`.
`PIVOT` turns distinct values of a column into separate columns (cross-tab); it does not compute running/rolling values.

da-2026-2-da-46.shortcut: Rolling / running / ranking per row ⇒ window function ⇒ `OVER(...)`.
pitfalls: Picking ROLLUP because it is the best-known "OLAP" extension of GROUP BY — it computes subtotals, not moving windows.
da-2026-2-da-46.verification: Only the window form keeps row count unchanged: `SELECT COUNT(*)` of the query above equals the row count of `daily_sales`, which no GROUP BY / PIVOT query guarantees.

steps.body:
With $
abla f(x^*)=0$:
$$f(x^*+h) = f(x^*) + \underbrace{
abla f(x^*)^Th}_{=0} + 	frac12 h^T
abla^2 f(x^*)h + o(\lVert hVert^2).$$

steps.title: Positive definite ⇒ strict local minimum
steps.body: If $H=\nabla^2 f(x^*)$ is positive definite, $h^THh \ge \lambda_{\min}\lVert h\rVert^2$ with $\lambda_{\min} > 0$. For small $h \ne 0$ the quadratic term dominates the remainder, so $f(x^*+h) > f(x^*)$: a **strict local minimum** — option (C).

steps.title: What the other cases give
steps.body:
- Negative definite: $h^THh<0$ for all $h\ne0$ ⇒ strict local **maximum**.
- Indefinite: some directions go up, others down ⇒ **saddle point**.
- Singular: some eigenvalue is $0$, so the test is **inconclusive** (e.g. $x^4$, $-x^4$ and $x^3$ all have $f\,''(0)=0$).

da-2026-2-da-48.approach: Find the fewest nodes $N(h)$ an AVL tree of height $h$ can have: $N(h)=N(h-1)+N(h-2)+1$, a Fibonacci-type recurrence, so $N(h)\approx\varphi^h$ and the height is at most $\log_\varphi n \approx 1.44\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Sparsest AVL tree of height h
steps.body:
To minimise nodes for a given height $h$, the root's subtrees should have heights $h-1$ and $h-2$ (the most unbalanced allowed), each itself sparsest:
$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1,\quad N(0)=1,\; N(1)=2.$$
Values: $1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, \dots$

steps.title: Solve the recurrence
steps.body: Adding 1: $N(h)+1 = (N(h-1)+1) + (N(h-2)+1)$, so $N(h)+1 = F_{h+3}$ (Fibonacci). Since $F_k \approx \varphi^k/\sqrt5$ with $\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618$, we get $n \ge N(h) \gtrsim \varphi^{h}$.

steps.title: Invert to bound the height
steps.body:
$h \lesssim \log_\varphi n = \dfrac{\log_2 n}{\log_2 \varphi} = \dfrac{\log_2 n}{0.694} \approx 1.44\log_2 n$.
So the worst-case height of an AVL tree with $n$ nodes is $\approx 1.44\log_2 n$, i.e. $\Theta(\log n)$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: From $N(h) = N(h-1)+N(h-2)+1 \approx \varphi^h$: $h \le \log_\varphi n \approx 1.44\log_2 n$.
$\Theta(n)$ is the worst case of an *unbalanced* BST (a chain); the AVL balance condition rules it out.
Too small: a binary tree with $n$ nodes has height at least $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, so $\Theta(\log\log n)$ is impossible.

da-2026-2-da-49.approach: Ridge regression adds the squared $L_2$ norm of the weight vector to the least-squares loss: $\min_w \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 + \lambda\sum_j w_j^2$. The penalty is the sum of squared weights.

steps.title: Write the ridge objective
steps.body:
$$J(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}(y_i - x_i^Tw)^2 + \lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2,\qquad \lVert w\rVert_2^2 = \sum_j w_j^2,\; \lambda>0.$$
The penalised quantity is $\sum_j w_j^2$ — option (A).

steps.title: Why it shrinks the weights
steps.body: Setting $\nabla J = 0$: $-2X^T(y-Xw) + 2\lambda w = 0 \Rightarrow w = (X^TX+\lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty$. Adding $\lambda I$ inflates every eigenvalue of $X^TX$ by $\lambda$, so each component (in the eigenbasis) is multiplied by $\frac{d_j}{d_j+\lambda} < 1$: coefficients shrink smoothly toward 0 but rarely become exactly 0.

steps.title: Contrast with Lasso
steps.body: Penalising $\sum_j \lvert w_j\rvert$ ($L_1$) is **Lasso**, which can set weights exactly to zero (feature selection). Rank and condition number are not penalty terms in either method.

answer.value: The sum of squared weights $\sum_j w_j^2$ — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Ridge penalty is $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = \lambda\sum_j w_j^2$.
Sum of absolute values is the $L_1$ penalty of Lasso, not Ridge.
The rank of the feature matrix is a property of the data, not a function of the weights; it is not penalised.
Ridge *improves* the conditioning of $X^TX$ as a side effect, but the condition number is not the penalty term.

pitfalls: Swapping the Ridge and Lasso penalties.

A singular Hessian makes the second-order test inconclusive: $x^4$ (min), $-x^4$ (max), $x^3$ (neither) all have zero second derivative at 0.
Positive definite ⇒ $h^THh > 0$ for all $h \ne 0$ ⇒ $f$ strictly increases in every direction ⇒ strict local minimum.
Negative definite gives a strict local maximum.

da-2026-2-da-55.shortcut: One variable analogue: $f'(x^*)=0$ and $f''(x^*)>0$ ⇒ minimum. "Positive second derivative" generalises to "positive definite Hessian".
pitfalls: Thinking positive *semi*definite is enough for a strict minimum — it is only a necessary condition.
Calling a singular Hessian a minimum.
da-2026-2-da-55.verification: $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ has $H=2I$ (positive definite) and a strict minimum at the origin; $f=x^2-y^2$ has $H=\mathrm{diag}(2,-2)$ (indefinite) and a saddle there.
